blocks.text: But they marveled at him like the little birds that surround the little owl. Lucian in the Harmonides: Ἔνθα ἂν καὶ νῦν φανῇς, συνδέουσιν ἐπί σε πάντες, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τὴν [III, 37] γλαῦκα τὰ ὄρνεα [entha an kai nyn phanēs, syndeousin epi se pantes, hōsper epi tēn glauka ta ornea]; Wherever you are seen, all run together to you, as other birds to the little owl. Dio Chrysostom says the same of it in the Olympic oration, right at the beginning: Ἐκείνην περιέπουσι τὰ ἄλλα ὄρνεα, ὅταν δὲ ἴδῃ μόνον, τὰ μὲν καθιζόμενα ἐγγὺς, τὰ δὲ κύκλῳ περιπετόμενα [ekeinēn periepousi ta alla ornea, hotan de idē monon, ta men kathizomena engys, ta de kyklō peripetomena], etc. Οἱ δὲ ἄνθρωποί φασιν, ὅτι θαυμάζει τὴν γλαῦκα τὰ ὄρνεα [hoi de anthrōpoi phasin, hoti thaumazei tēn glauka ta ornea]; The other birds follow her, and when they merely see her, some sit down near her, others fly round her in a circle, etc. And men say that the birds marvel at the little owl. The makers of fables invent another reason, namely that the birds marvel at her and are stupefied at the sight of her because of a horrible crime she once committed. Servius on the first book of the Georgics: Nyctimene, after she had lain with her father and recognized the crime, hid herself in the woods and fled the light, where by the will of the gods she was changed into a bird (the little owl), which, because of so great a crime, is an object of wonder to all birds. On Nyctimene see more in the second book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, and in Hyginus, Fables 204 and 253. However fabulous these things may be, it is nonetheless established that the other birds are stupefied when they see the little owl, and, held fast by that stupor, are caught. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 1: Τὰ ἄλλα ὀρνίθια τὴν γλαῦκα περιπέτεται, ὃ καλεῖται θαυμάζειν· καὶ προσπετόμενα τίλλουσι. διὸ οἱ ὀρνιθο- [col. 291] θῆραι θηρεύουσιν αὐτῇ παντοδαπὰ ὀρνίθια [ta alla ornithia tēn glauka peripetetai, ho kaleitai thaumazein; kai prospetomena tillousi. dio hoi ornithothērai thēreuousin autē pantodapa ornithia]; The other little birds fly around the little owl, which is called marveling; and flying at her they pluck at her. For this reason fowlers use her to catch little birds of every kind. Hence Aelian, History of Animals, book 1, chapter 29: Αἱμύλον ζῶον, καὶ ἐοικὸς ταῖς φαρμακίσιν ἡ γλαύξ [haimylon zōon, kai eoikos tais pharmakisin hē glaux]; The little owl is a wily animal, and like sorceresses. And after explaining that it is carried about by fowlers to serve them as a decoy: Νύκτωρ μὲν αὐτοῖς ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ τῇ φωνῇ, οἱονεί τινι ἐπαοιδῇ γοητείας ὑπεσπαρμένη, αἱμύλου τε, καὶ θελκτικῆς, τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἕλκει, καὶ καθίζει πλησίον ἑαυτῆς· ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ θήρατρα ἕτερα τοῖς ὄρνισι προσήει [nyktōr men autois agrypnei, kai tē phōnē, hoionei tini epaoidē goēteias hypesparmenē, haimylou te, kai thelktikēs, tous ornithas helkei, kai kathizei plēsion heautēs; ēdē de kai en hēmera thēratra hetera tois ornisi prosēei] (read προσφέρει [prospherei]) μωκωμένη, καὶ ἄλλοτε ἄλλην ἰδέαν προσώπου στρέφουσα, ἐφ᾽ ὧν αἱροῦνται, καὶ περιμένουσιν οἱ νέοι πάντες ὄρνιθες, ἠρημένοι δέει [mōkōmenē, kai allote allēn idean prosōpou strephousa, eph᾽ hōn hairountai, kai perimenousin hoi neoi pantes ornithes, ērēmenoi deei] (read θέᾳ [thea]) καὶ μοίλᾳ γε [kai moila ge] (read αἱμυλίᾳ γε [haimylia ge]) ἰσχυρῶς, ἐξ ὧν ἐκείνη μορφάζει [ischyrōs, ex hōn ekeinē morphazei]; By night she keeps watch for them, and with her voice, as with a kind of magic song, coaxing and alluring, secretly scattered abroad, she draws the birds and makes them sit beside her. By day she offers the birds other enticements, mocking them and turning her face into one shape after another, by which all the younger little birds are caught and held, detained by the spectacle and the enticements of the forms into which she transforms herself. Philes, chapter 21 On Animals:

Αἱμύλιον ἡ γλαὺξ ἡ φιλέσπερος φύσει. Σκοπεῖν γὰρ εἰκὸς τῆς πανούργου τὸν δόλον. Μωκωμένη τὰς ὄρνις ἡμέρας ὅλης, Καὶ ποικίλη στρέφουσα μορφῇ τὴν θέαν, Σαίνει τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὑποπτέρων γένη. [Haimylion hē glaux hē philesperos physei. Skopein gar eikos tēs panourgou ton dolon. Mōkōmenē tas ornis hēmeras holēs, Kai poikilē strephousa morphē tēn thean, Sainei ta mikra tōn hypopterōn genē.]

[III, 38] The evening-loving little owl is of a wily nature. It is worth observing her tricks. Mocking the birds the whole day, and displaying herself to be looked at in various forms, she fawns upon the smaller winged creatures. Palladius, book 10, chapter 12: Now (in the month of September) the fowling with the little owl is prepared in the snares, together with the other instruments of capture, so that it may be practised around the Calends of October. Petrus Crescentiensis, On Plants and Animals, book 10, chapter 16, which is On the gimo and the gimetta, that is, the male and female little owl: The other birds marvel at them and long to see them, as something new and unusual. For this reason men, seeing the other birds flying around the gimo and gimetta and gazing at them with the greatest eagerness, devised a new method of fowling: namely, by setting out these birds as a spectacle, to catch for themselves the others thus lured, with birdlime or nets. Rightly, then, is the little owl called תנשמת thinsemeth, as being astounding and wonderful, that is, to those little birds which, struck with stupor, it draws to itself. Accordingly not only the Hebrews, but among our own scholars Arias, Castalio, Schindler etc. render it "little owl". And the two Chaldee versions, the Syriac and the Samaritan follow the same. As a corollary I may add a not unpleasing little fable about the ugliness of the little owl, taken from the Iambics of Gregory of Nazianzus, Poem 22:

Τὴν γλαῦκ᾽ ἐπέσκωπτέ τις· ἡ δ᾽ ἐφύγγανε Τῶν σκομμάτων ἕκαστον εὐστόχῳ λόγῳ. Ὅσσον κάρηνον! Τοῦ Διὸς δὲ πήλικον. Ἡ γλαυκότης δέ! Τοῦτο τῆς Γλαυκώπιδος· Φθέγγῃ δύσηχον. Ἡ δὲ κίττα καὶ πλέον· Τὸ λεπτοποῦν πῶς; Ψὴρ δὲ σοί τι φαίνεται; Ἐπεὶ δὲ πάντα ῥαδίως διέδρασε Ἑνὶ κρατεῖται, καὶ σοφή περ οὖσ᾽ ὅμως. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς σοφὴ, σκόπησον· ὡς τούτων μὲν ἓν Ἑνὶ πρόεστι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἅπαντα καὶ λίαν· Γλαυκὴ, δύσηχος, λεπτόπους, βαρύκρανος. Τούτοις ἀπῆλθεν ἐντραπεῖσ᾽ ἡ φιλτάτη. [Tēn glauk᾽ episkōpte tis; hē d᾽ ephyngane Tōn skommatōn hekaston eustochō logō. Hosson karēnon! Tou Dios de pēlikon. Hē glaukotēs de! Touto tēs Glaukōpidos; Phthengē dysēchon. Hē de kitta kai pleon; To leptopoun pōs? Psēr de soi ti phainetai? Epei de panta rhadiōs dierdrase Heni krateitai, kai sophē per ous᾽ homōs. All᾽, hōs sophē, skopēson; hōs toutōn men hen Heni proesti, soi d᾽ hapanta kai lian; Glaukē, dysēchos, leptopous, barykranos. Toutois apēlthen entrapeis᾽ hē philtatē.]
